extracted.intended_audience: general literate public; readers of The Spectator (early-18th-century periodical audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of short moral, satirical, and literary essays and letters (The Spectator, 1712) offering moral reflections, social observation, and examples of poetic imitation. Material is aimed at general readers and contains embedded prescriptive remarks about language, manners, and literary practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use words with clear, distinct ideas; define moral terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Locke's identified abuse: using words 'without clear and distinct Ideas' and the recommendation that 'a Definition ... is the only way whereby the precise Meaning of Moral Words can be known.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using terms without precise ideas attached; in moral discourse especially, give definitions so terms retain fixed meaning. Consequence of failing: 'the Result of our Contemplations and Reasonings ... must needs be very confused and absurd.' Examples in the text: common confusion over the words 'Modesty' and 'Assurance'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent in application of terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Locke's second abuse of words: being 'so inconstant and unsteady in the Application of them, that we sometimes use them to signify one Idea, sometimes another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same word to signify the same idea across a discourse; do not shift senses between uses. In practice, maintain semantic consistency to avoid confusing arguments and misinterpretation. The author illustrates the problem by showing how 'modesty' and 'assurance' are commonly applied to different ideas than their proper senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore and state the true meaning of contested moral terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When words (e.g., 'Modesty' and 'Assurance') are broadly misused, explicitly define them: e.g. 'Modesty: The Reflection of an Ingenuous Mind...'; 'Assurance: the Faculty of possessing a Man's self, or of saying and doing indifferent things without any Uneasiness or Emotion in the Mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing moral description or character portraits, give clear definitions and contrast commonly confused senses. Use examples and counterexamples (e.g., the prince who blushed in the Senate) to illustrate the defined senses and their moral value. Point out consequences of confusion (e.g., modesty mistaken for sheepishness; assurance misread as impudence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical exaggeration and mock-catalogue to lampoon sentimental tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: To parody the fashion of 'dying for love' and sentimental melodrama, assemble an absurd, highly-specific 'Bill of Mortality' listing comically fantastic deaths (e.g., 'Lysander, slain at a Puppet-show', 'Damon, struck thro' the Heart by a Diamond Necklace').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hyperbole, vivid concrete incidents, named characters, and absurd-but-specific set-pieces to expose and ridicule overwrought sentimental conventions. A mock-catalogue or list of ludicrously detailed misfortunes is an effective satirical device for this purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of classical models and elevated diction for sacred/epic themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Pope's preface: the poem 'MESSIAH' is 'Written in Imitation of Virgil's POLLIO' and composed from passages of Isaiah — an explicit model-based, classical approach to sacred subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing sacred or grand themes, one acceptable practice is to imitate classical forms (e.g., Virgilian eclogue/epic diction), to fuse elevated classical style with biblical/allusive material. Techniques shown: classical invocations ('Ye Nymphs of Solyma! begin the Song'), lofty imagery, and direct incorporation or paraphrase of scriptural passages to achieve solemnity and grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional description of social accomplishments as signs of refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical guidance on education/manners: cultivate 'an humble courteous Mind, accompanied with a graceful becoming Mein' and teach accomplishments (e.g., dancing) which display 'the Beauty and Spirit there is in regular Motion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pieces about education or character, emphasize concrete accomplishments (household knowledge, dancing, genteel table manners, how to present a snuff-box, place a patch) as markers of refinement. When describing teachers/masters, note both technical skill and the social graces they impart. Use such particulars to signal social status and moral worth in character portrayal.
